description: Aragonese-ruled Sicily (1282–1409) that emerged from the Sicilian Vespers revolt against Angevin rule; the protracted War of the Sicilian Vespers demonstrated the limits of Angevin overreach and established Aragonese Mediterranean dominance, while the island's position as a grain-exporting hub and naval base made it strategically vital for Italian and western Mediterranean politics.

temporal.notes: Island kingdom after Sicilian Vespers; Aragonese branch

lifecycle_phases.description: The Sicilian Vespers (March 30, 1282), a spontaneous massacre of French Angevin soldiers in Palermo, and the subsequent War of the Sicilian Vespers (1282–1302) establishes the Aragonese line on Sicily. Peter III of Aragon's victory confirms Aragonese Sicily; the island remains separate from the mainland Angevin kingdom. The Peace of Caltabellotta (1302) ends the war with Sicily recognized as an Aragonese possession.

The Aragonese kingdom of Sicily (Trinacria) is reincorporated into the Crown of Aragon (1372) under Martin I. Sicily serves as the breadbasket of the western Mediterranean, exporting grain to the Italian cities. Alfonso V conquers Naples (1442), briefly reuniting Sicily and the mainland; after his death (1458), Sicily reverts to the Aragonese crown while Naples goes to his illegitimate son Ferrante.

rise_factors.description: Sicily's volcanic soil produced the highest grain yields in the Mediterranean; Sicilian grain exports sustained the urban populations of Genoa, Florence, and other Italian cities, making control of Sicily an economic necessity for any western Mediterranean power

Peter III of Aragon's claim came through his Hohenstaufen wife Constance; the Sicilian Vespers uprising (1282) gave him the island's support, turning what would have been conquest into liberation, the most favorable possible basis for rule

The Crown of Aragon possessed the most advanced naval infrastructure in the western Mediterranean; Catalan merchants and the Aragonese war fleet made Sicily a hub of eastern trade, supplanting the Angevin commercial system

Sicily's wheat plains were the breadbasket of the Mediterranean; Aragonese control of this export surplus funded the fleet, paid the army, and attracted Catalan merchant capital that integrated Sicily into the broader Aragonese commercial empire

The Sicilian Vespers uprising of 1282 expelled the French Angevins; the Sicilians invited Peter III of Aragon, creating the Aragonese Kingdom of Sicily as a separate state from the Angevin Kingdom of Naples.

decline_factors.description: Alfonso V's death (1458) without legitimate heirs to his Italian territories separated Sicily from Naples; the resulting fragmentation of his Mediterranean empire weakened Aragonese strategic coherence

Aragonese kings ruling from Barcelona or Valencia treated Sicily as a secondary possession; local viceroy governance was susceptible to baronial capture, and without the personal presence of the king, central authority eroded

The Sicilian barons who had welcomed Aragonese rule expected rewards; the resulting baronial power undermined royal income and justice, creating the endemic feudal anarchy that made the island ungovernable during periods of weak central rule
The union of Castile and Aragon under Ferdinand and Isabella (1469) integrated Sicily into a much larger Iberian-dominated Mediterranean empire, ending its distinct Aragonese royal dynasty.

Charles VIII's invasion of Italy in 1494, using Sicily as a staging point, drew the kingdom into the Italian Wars between France and Spain; the eventual Habsburg victory locked Sicily into Spanish imperial governance for over 150 years.
